Web page |  You can use a robots.txt file for web pages (HTML, PDF, or other [non-media formats that Google can read](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/indexable-file-types)), to manage crawling traffic if you think your server will be overwhelmed by requests from Google's crawler, or to avoid crawling unimportant or similar pages on your site.

**If your web page is blocked with a robots.txt file** , its URL can still appear in search results, but the search result [won't have a description](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7489871).

item.name: AI safety
item.description: Operation of AI systems that does not endanger human life, health, property, or the environment; improved through responsible design, deployment practices, simulation and in-domain testing, monitoring, and human intervention.
item.grounding_span:
Other practical approaches for AI safety often relate to rigorous simulation and in-domain
testing, real-time monitoring, and the ability to shut down, modify, or have human inter-
vention into systems that deviate from intended or expected functionality.

item.name: safety risks
item.description: Risks of AI systems leading to injury, death, or other endangerment; prioritized by context and severity.
item.grounding_span:
Different types of safety risks may require tailored AI risk management approaches based
on context and the severity of potential risks presented.

item.name: AI risk management
item.description: Tailored approaches to managing AI risk, whose urgency and thoroughness scale with the severity of potential harm and which should align with sector-specific guidance.
item.grounding_span:
Different types of safety risks may require tailored AI risk management approaches based
on context and the severity of potential risks presented.

item.name: resilience
item.description: Ability of an AI system and its ecosystem to withstand unexpected adverse events or changes, maintain function and structure, degrade safely, and return to normal function.
item.grounding_span: Security and resilience are related but distinct characteristics.

item.name: security
item.description: Maintenance of confidentiality, integrity, and availability through protection mechanisms preventing unauthorized access and use; encompasses resilience plus protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, and recover from attacks.
item.grounding_span:
While resilience is the abil-
ity to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event, security includes re-
silience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover
from attacks.

item.name: transparency
item.description: Extent to which information about an AI system and its outputs is available to individuals interacting with it, tailored to lifecycle stage and to the role or knowledge of AI actors.
item.grounding_span:
Meaningful transparency provides access to appropriate levels
of information based on the stage of the AI lifecycle and tailored to the role or knowledge
of AI actors or individuals interacting with or using the AI system.

item.name: accountability
item.description: Answerability for the outcomes of AI systems; presupposes transparency and varies across cultural, legal, sectoral, and societal contexts.
item.grounding_span:
The role of AI actors should be considered when seeking accountability for the outcomes of
AI systems.

item.name: explainability
item.description: Representation of the mechanisms underlying an AI system's operation; answers how a decision was made.
item.grounding_span:
Risk from lack of explainability may be managed by describing how AI systems function,
with descriptions tailored to individual differences such as the user’s role, knowledge, and
skill level.

item.name: interpretability
item.description: Meaning of an AI system's output in the context of its designed functional purpose; answers why a decision was made and what it means to the user.
item.grounding_span:
Page 16
NIST AI 100-1 AI RMF 1.0
Risks to interpretability often can be addressed by communicating a description of why
an AI system made a particular prediction or recommendation.

item.name: AI actors
item.description: Parties whose role is considered when seeking accountability for AI system outcomes and to whom transparency is tailored.
item.grounding_span:
The role of AI actors should be considered when seeking accountability for the outcomes of
AI systems.

item.name: provenance of training data
item.description: Maintenance of the origin record of training data, and attribution of system decisions to subsets of it, as an aid to transparency and accountability.

item.grounding_span:
Maintaining the provenance of training data and supporting attribution of the AI system’s
decisions to subsets of training data can assist with both transparency and accountability.

item.name: ROOTS
item.grounding_span:
Without proper doc-
umentation and search tools like ROOTS (Piktus
et al., 2023) it is very difficult for any researcher to
actually know whether their datasets are compro-
mised on a given model.

This position paper de-
fines different levels of data contamination and
argues for a community effort, including the
development of automatic and semi-automatic
measures to detect when data from a bench-
mark was exposed to a model, and suggestions
for flagging papers with conclusions that are
compromised by data contamination.

The worst kind of data contamination
happens when a Large Language Model (LLM)
is trained on the test split of a benchmark, and
then evaluated in the same benchmark.

In this case, it has
been shown that the high memorization abilities of
LLMs can be used to generate portions of the train-
ing texts (Carlini et al., 2021; Magar and Schwartz,
2022).

This solution involves a registry of contamination
cases1, collaborative manual work and research on
automatic approaches.

In addition, conferences
should devise mechanisms to ensure that papers
1Such as the LM Contamination Index https://

discovered after publication.

item.name: SFV
item.description: The framework addressing the asymmetry whereby coherent text can be produced from any input state, making state degradation invisible.
item.grounding_span:
This is the fundamental asymmetry that SFV 
addresses: the same property that makes language models useful, their ability to produce coherent 
text from any input state, is the property that makes state degradation invisible.

item.name: monitoring layer
item.description: The layer inside which an SFV threat can hide if built on stochastic components.
item.grounding_span:
INC-006 was a deterministic bug, legible and fixable; had the checker 
been built on stochastic components, the same failure would have been invisible for the same

item.name: stochastic tax
item.description: The cost incurred by each stochastic component in a pipeline or verification layer; applies to retrieval design as well.
item.grounding_span:
The fidelity gain is a direct consequence of reducing unnec-
essary stochastic components in the pipeline, the stochastic tax applied to retrieval design.

item.name: Deterministic retrieval
item.description: A design countermeasure using deterministic database lookups so every query to the same concept returns the same expert judgment.
item.grounding_span: Deterministic retrieval as a design countermeasure has independent empirical grounding.

item.name: retrieval-augmented generation
item.description: Retrieval by embedding similarity, contrasted with deterministic lookup and reported at lower fidelity.
item.grounding_span:
A 
statistical consultation pipeline achieved 91.2% fidelity to authoritative data sources across 353 
verifiable claims using deterministic database lookups for expert judgment retrieval, compared 
to 74.6% across 355 claims for retrieval-augmented generation using embedding similarity (Webb 
2026a).

item.name: retrieval variance
item.description: The variance embedding-based retrieval introduces, eliminated by deterministic retrieval.
item.grounding_span:
The difference is attributable to a single architectural choice: deterministic retrieval elimi-
nates the retrieval variance that embedding-based approaches introduce.

checklist items (canonical glossary, external decision log, reconciliation checks) are ordered first 
because their absence leaves the most dangerous threats unmonitored.

characteristics of linkage-eligible survey participants differ from the nationally representative survey 
population.

item.name: total measurement error
item.description: The aggregate error the CPI program seeks not to increase when substituting alternative data for traditional collection.
item.grounding_span:
The technical experts group, which consists 
of senior BLS economists and statisticians, are working with BLS staff to develop a new methodology to 
ensure that the use of alternative data does not increase the total measurement error relative to 
traditional methods of data collection or previously implemented non-traditional methods.

item.name: cost-effectiveness
item.description: An additional evaluation question the CPI program considers alongside the DQ framework dimensions.
item.grounding_span:
For example, to 
evaluate the dimension of relevance, BLS adds “Are the data a relevant input to our data products and 
measurement objective?” For evaluation of timeliness, the CPI program asks itself, “Are the data 
representative of the index reference period?” The CPI program also considers an additional question 
about cost-effectiveness to complement the DQ framework.

item.name: alternative data approval process

item.grounding_span:

approval groups, technical experts and the approval board.

traveled over 300 billion vehicle miles.20 The FMCSA conducts its safety mission by registering motor 
carriers and other entities and enforcing regulations, through inspections and investigations, which 
maintains the balance between supply chain efficiency and roadway safety.

An inspection is an examination of an individual 
commercial motor vehicle (CMV) and/or driver by an authorized safety inspector.20 The FMCSA, in 
collaboration with its state partners, conducts approximately 3.5 million inspections annually across the 
United States.20 The inspection determines whether the driver and/or the CMV is in compliance with the 
Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations (FMCSRs) or the Hazardous Materials Regulations (HMRs), as 
appropriate.

item.name: Granularity
item.description: Whether the inspection records carry an adequate level of detail for their use.
item.grounding_span:
Granularity – The inspection records provide an adequate level of detail in accordance with the North 
American Standard Inspection Program, which was developed by the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance 
to improve the safe operation of commercial motor vehicles by establishing a uniform and reciprocal 
roadside inspection and enforcement process for commercial motor vehicles.

item.name: Accuracy and Reliability
item.description: Objectivity sub-dimension; here rated by two criteria applied to the inspection record.
item.grounding_span:
Objectivity 
Accuracy and Reliability– The accuracy of the inspection record is rated on two criteria: (1) inspection 
record matching a carrier registered with the FMCSA in the MCMIS; and (2) Vehicle Identification 
Number (VIN) meeting a validation criterion.21 While the two criteria provide a rudimentary level of 
quality control, they do not ensure holistic quality across the inspection record.

item.name: Coherence
item.description: Objectivity sub-dimension; consistency of inspection records, driven by validations built into inspection software.
item.grounding_span:
Coherence – The North American Standard Inspection Program provides a good level of guidance to 
ensure coherence in inspection records.

item.name: Scientific Integrity
item.description: Integrity sub-dimension; inspections follow prescribed procedures and record observed facts against validation criteria.
item.grounding_span:
Integrity 
Scientific Integrity– All inspections are conducted in accordance with minimum inspection procedures, 
standards, and requirements described in the North American Standard Inspection Program.

item.name: Credibility
item.description: Integrity sub-dimension; confidence in the personnel and process that capture and validate inspection data.
item.grounding_span:
Credibility – All inspections are conducted by inspectors who are federal or state law enforcement 
officers.

item.name: Computer and Physical Security
item.description: Integrity sub-dimension; protection of inspection records via cloud databases, role-based access control and authentication.
item.grounding_span:
Computer and Physical Security – All inspection records are housed in cloud-based databases that serve 
applications that implement role-based access controls to furnish the inspection records to users on a 
need-to-know basis.

item.name: Confidentiality
item.description: Integrity sub-dimension; access controls limiting carriers to their own records while enforcement personnel see all.
item.grounding_span:
Confidentiality – Access controls are in place to ensure that (1) motor carriers have access to only their 
inspection records, and (2) enforcement personnel, including federal and state inspection personnel, 
have access to all inspection records to review.

item.name: SafeSpect
item.description: FMCSA web-based inspection application providing a single sign-on, one-stop interface for conducting and processing inspections.
item.grounding_span:
SafeSpect provides a one-stop shop to the inspection community 
for all their inspection needs, which promotes accuracy by allowing the inspectors to log in once and 
conduct the entire inspection, from cradle to grave, without ever logging into another application.

item.name: FCSM Framework for Data Quality
item.anchor: FCSM Framework for Data Quality serves
item.grounding_span:
Introduction: This case study examines how the FCSM Framework for Data Quality serves as a tool to 
determine the utility of administrative data in determining program effectiveness and provides 
considerations for the data’s use that are paramount to upholding rigor and ethics as principles of 
program evaluation.

The NDNH is a repository of employment, unemployment insurance (UI), and quarterly wage data 
maintained by the Office of Child Support Enforcement (OCSE) at the HHS.

Thus, agencies often rely on administrative data that are already collected by the 
government for a different purpose and use the data to aggregate program outcomes and estimate 
policy impacts.

It is imperative 
that researchers are transparent about the fitness for use of existing data for program evaluation, to 
strengthen credibility of study design and findings, and to account for other factors including data 
privacy.

It is important to 
note that this case study examines data quality of the NDNH for a specific study and is not meant to 
serve as a review of the data quality of the NDNH itself.

The NDNH combines three types of data: employment information on all newly hired employees as 
reported by employers, quarterly wage information on individual employees, and UI information on 
individuals who received or applied for unemployment benefits.

The database, authorized in 
Sec. 453 of the Social Security Miscellaneous Amendments Act of 1996, was originally designed to help 
state and federal agencies locate noncustodial parents to establish and enforce child support orders, 
particularly across state jurisdictions.

The use 
of the NDNH requires the allocation of time to develop and execute memorandums of understanding 
between three federal agencies.

Use of the NDNH also requires full reimbursement of the costs of data 
matching services.

dataset:

• Earnings data collected by the IRS for tax purposes

• Earnings data collected by the state unemployment insurance agencies, housed by each state 
• Earnings data contained within the NDNH and obtained from states and federal agencies by HHS  
• Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics (LEHD) program at the U.S. Census Bureau

In order to facilitate program evaluations such as the TAP impact evaluation, the DOL conducted a 
review of eight sources of earnings data.39 The data source review included:  
• Earnings data collected by the IRS for tax purposes  
• Earnings data maintained by the Social Security Administration in the master earnings file  
• Earnings data collected by the state unemployment insurance agencies, housed by each state 
• Earnings data contained within the NDNH and obtained from states and federal agencies by HHS  
• Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics (LEHD) program at the U.S. Census Bureau

item.name: AI RMF
item.grounding_span:
The AI RMF is intended to be practical, to adapt to the AI landscape as AI technologies
continue to develop, and to be operationalized by organizations in varying degrees and
capacities so society can benefit from AI while also being protected from its potential
harms.

AI actors are defined by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
(OECD) as “those who play an active role in the AI system lifecycle, including organiza-
tions and individuals that deploy or operate AI” [OECD (2019) Artificial Intelligence in
Society—OECD iLibrary] (See Appendix A).

The Framework is intended to be
voluntary, rights-preserving, non-sector-specific, and use-case agnostic, providing flexibil-
ity to organizations of all sizes and in all sectors and throughout society to implement the
approaches in the Framework.

The Framework is designed to equip organizations and individuals – referred to here as
AI actors – with approaches that increase the trustworthiness of AI systems, and to help
foster the responsible design, development, deployment, and use of AI systems over time.

The AI RMF is intended to be practical, to adapt to the AI landscape as AI technologies
continue to develop, and to be operationalized by organizations in varying degrees and
capacities so society can benefit from AI while also being protected from its potential

AI systems can also present new risks to privacy by allowing inference to identify
individuals or previously private information about individuals.

Privacy-enhancing technologies (“PETs”) for AI, as well as data minimizing methods such
as de-identification and aggregation for certain model outputs, can support design for
privacy-enhanced AI systems.

Standards of fairness can be complex and difficult to define be-
cause perceptions of fairness differ among cultures and may shift depending on application.
Systems in which harmful biases are mitigated are not necessarily fair.

For example, systems in which predictions are somewhat balanced across demographic
groups may still be inaccessible to individuals with disabilities or affected by the digital
divide or may exacerbate existing disparities or systemic biases.

Page 17
NIST AI 100-1 AI RMF 1.0
Bias is broader than demographic balance and data representativeness.

NIST has identified
three major categories of AI bias to be considered and managed: systemic, computational
and statistical, and human-cognitive.

Each of these can occur in the absence of prejudice,
partiality, or discriminatory intent.

Computational and statistical biases can be present in AI datasets
and algorithmic processes, and often stem from systematic errors due to non-representative
samples.

Human-cognitive biases are omnipresent
in decision-making processes across the AI lifecycle and system use, including the design,
implementation, operation, and maintenance of AI.

Bias exists in many forms and can become ingrained in the automated systems that help
make decisions about our lives.

item.name: dcat:Catalog
item.description: A catalog, which is a dataset in which each individual item is a metadata record describing some resource; its scope is collections of metadata about datasets, data services, or other resource types.
item.grounding_span: - `dcat:Catalog` represents a catalog, which is a dataset in which each individual item is a metadata record describing some resource; the scope of `dcat:Catalog` is collections of metadata about **datasets**, **data services**, or other resource types.

item.name: dcat:Resource
item.description: A dataset, a data service or any other resource that may be described by a metadata record in a catalog; not intended to be used directly, it is the parent class of the other cataloged resource classes and an extension point.
item.grounding_span: - `dcat:Resource` represents a dataset, a data service or any other resource that may be described by a metadata record in a catalog. This class is not intended to be used directly, but is the parent class of `dcat:Dataset`, `dcat:DataService` and `dcat:Catalog`. Resources in a catalog should be instances of one of these classes, or of a sub-class of these, or of a sub-class of `dcat:Resource` defined in a DCAT profile or other DCAT application. `dcat:Resource` is actually an extension point for defining a catalog of any kind of resources. `dcat:Dataset` and `dcat:DataService` can be used for datasets and services which are not documented in any catalog.

item.name: dcat:Dataset
item.description: A collection of data, published or curated by a single agent or identifiable community; the notion is broad and inclusive of resource types from all communities.
item.grounding_span: - `dcat:Dataset` represents a collection of data, published or curated by a single agent or identifiable community. The notion of dataset in DCAT is broad and inclusive, with the intention of accommodating resource types arising from all communities. Data comes in many forms including numbers, text, pixels, imagery, sound and other multi-media, and potentially other types, any of which might be collected into a dataset.

item.grounding_span: - `dcat:Catalog` represents a catalog, which is a dataset in which each individual item is a metadata record describing some resource; the scope of `dcat:Catalog` is collections of metadata about **datasets**, **data services**, or other resource types.

- `dcat:Resource` represents a dataset, a data service or any other resource that may be described by a metadata record in a catalog. This class is not intended to be used directly, but is the parent class of `dcat:Dataset`, `dcat:DataService` and `dcat:Catalog`. Resources in a catalog should be instances of one of these classes, or of a sub-class of these, or of a sub-class of `dcat:Resource` defined in a DCAT profile or other DCAT application. `dcat:Resource` is actually an extension point for defining a catalog of any kind of resources. `dcat:Dataset` and `dcat:DataService` can be used for datasets and services which are not documented in any catalog.

- `dcat:Dataset` represents a collection of data, published or curated by a single agent or identifiable community. The notion of dataset in DCAT is broad and inclusive, with the intention of accommodating resource types arising from all communities. Data comes in many forms including numbers, text, pixels, imagery, sound and other multi-media, and potentially other types, any of which might be collected into a dataset.
- `dcat:Distribution` represents an accessible form of a dataset such as a downloadable file.
- `dcat:DataService` represents a collection of operations accessible through an interface (API) that provide access to one or more datasets or data processing functions.
- `dcat:DatasetSeries` is a dataset that represents a collection of datasets that are published separately, but share some characteristics that group them.
- `dcat:CatalogRecord` represents a metadata record in the catalog, primarily concerning the registration information, such as who added the record and when.
A **DCAT profile** is a specification for a data catalog that adds additional constraints to DCAT.

item.name: version chain
item.description: A sequence of snapshots of a resource that dcat:previousVersion is used to specify.
item.grounding_span: | Usage note: | This property is meant to be used to specify a version chain, consisting of snapshots of a resource. The notion of version used by this property is limited to versions resulting from revisions occurring to a resource as part of its life-cycle. One of the typical cases here is representing the history of the versions of a dataset that have been released over time. |

item.name: lineage
item.description: The succession of resource versions in which a previous version sits.
item.grounding_span: | Definition: | The previous version of a resource in a lineage [PAV]. |

item.name: notion of version
item.description: The sense of 'version' a property assumes; DCAT's version properties use a narrower one than dcterms:hasVersion.
item.grounding_span: | Usage note: | This property is intended for relating a non-versioned or abstract resource to several versioned resources, e.g., snapshots [PAV]. The notion of version used by this property is limited to versions resulting from revisions occurring to a resource as part of its life-cycle. Therefore, its semantics is more specific than its super-property `dcterms:hasVersion`, which makes use of a broader notion of version, including editions and adaptations. |

item.name: data citation
item.description: The use case of relating a dataset to the scholarly publications and other resources that cite or point to it.
item.grounding_span: | Usage note: | In relation to the use case of data citation, when the cataloged resource is a dataset, the `dcterms:isReferencedBy` property allows to relate the dataset to the resources (such as scholarly publications) that cite or point to the dataset. Multiple `dcterms:isReferencedBy` properties can be used to indicate the dataset has been referenced by multiple publications, or other resources. |

item.claim_text: This class is optional and not all catalogs will use it.
item.grounding_span: | Usage note | This class is optional and not all catalogs will use it. It exists for catalogs where a distinction is made between metadata about a *dataset or service* and metadata about the *entry in the catalog about the dataset or service*. For example, the *publication date* property of the *dataset* reflects the date when the information was originally made available by the publishing agency, while the publication date of the *catalog record* is the date when the dataset was added to the catalog. In cases where both dates differ, or where only the latter is known, the *publication date* *SHOULD* only be specified for the catalog record. Notice that the W3C PROV Ontology [PROV-O] allows describing further provenance information such as the details of the process and the agent involved in a particular change to a dataset or its registration. |

In some cases all distributions of a dataset will be fully informationally equivalent, in the sense that lossless transformations between the representations are possible.

As a counter-example, budget data for different years would usually be modeled as different datasets, each with their own distributions, since all distributions of one dataset should broadly contain the same data.
Nevertheless, the question of whether different representations can be understood to be distributions of the same dataset, or distributions of different datasets, is application specific.

Information about licenses and rights *SHOULD* be provided on the level of Distribution. item.anchor: distinction between DRAI and data quality
item.grounding_span:

AI [63].

Data Quality Toolkit (DQT) [39] provides a suite of tools and functionalities to
streamline the preparation and cleaning of data.

DQT’s data quality report various dimensions of data quality metrics
defined by Sidi et al. [128] such as completeness, consistency, accuracy, and timeliness, along with suggestions for
improvement.

Ravi et al. [45] focus on the critical process of making experimental datasets FAIR (Findable, Accessible,
Interoperable, Reusable) for AI readiness.

payload.name: Table 2
payload.grounding_span:
In Table 2, we
provide a snapshot of all the dimensions and metrics discussed in this survey.

item.name: Heterogeneous Value Difference Metric (HVDM)
item.description: A distance metric used during imputation that handles both nominal and continuous data while preserving data distribution.
item.grounding_span: choosing appropriate distance metrics, such as Heterogeneous Value Difference Metric (HVDM) and Heterogeneous

item.name: Euclidean-Overlap Metri (HEOM)
item.description: A distance metric used during imputation that handles both nominal and continuous data while preserving data distribution.
item.grounding_span:
Euclidean-Overlap Metri (HEOM), which effectively handle both nominal and continuous data while preserving data
distribution during imputation.

item.name: completeness
item.description: A structured-data readiness dimension concerned with missing values, including missing data disguised with default values.
item.grounding_span: Another type of completeness targets missing data “disguised” with default values.

item.name: disguised missing values
item.description: Missing values encoded or represented so that they appear valid — e.g. a zero standing in for a missing entry — rather than being explicitly marked missing.
item.grounding_span:
Identifying explicitly missing
data is easy, while disguised missing values pose a greater challenge as they appear valid but are placeholders or
incorrect entries.

item.name: KNN imputation
item.description: A remedy for missing values recommended in the surveyed literature, used with suitable evaluation metrics.
item.grounding_span:
Summary: Metrics proposed by various researchers quantify the impact of missing values and suggest remedies such
as KNN imputation with suitable evaluation metrics.

item.name: Outliers
item.description: Data points that deviate significantly from the typical or expected values of a dataset and do not follow its general patterns.
item.grounding_span:
Outliers in a dataset refer to data points that significantly deviate from the typical or expected values
within the dataset.

item.name: plausibility
item.description: A metric discussed by Bors et al. for identifying outliers in datasets used by AI applications.
item.grounding_span:
[24] discuss the concept of plausibility as a metric to identify
outliers in datasets for AI applications, which can disrupt statistical analyses and modeling.

item.name: robust statistics
item.description: One of two main approaches to quantifying outliers; uses the median and the robust interquartile range estimator, which resist the influence of outliers.
item.grounding_span:
Data analysts employ two
main approaches to quantify the number of outliers: robust statistics and non-robust statistics.

item.name: non-robust statistics
item.description: Outlier quantification using the mean and standard deviation to identify entries deviating significantly from the mean.
item.grounding_span:
In contrast, non-robust
statistics involve using the mean and standard deviation to identify entries that deviate significantly from the mean.

item.name: Local Outlier Factor (LOF)
item.description: A density-based outlier metric that scores each data instance by comparing the density of its neighborhood with that of its neighboring instances.
item.grounding_span:
[26] introduce the Local Outlier Factor (LOF) as a metric for identifying outliers in a
dataset.

item.name: ILOF (Incremental Local Outlier Factor)
item.description: A method that uses the LOF metric to score an incoming data point in real time and updates the scores of existing points.
item.grounding_span:
Building on this foundation, Pokrajac et al. [107] introduced
the ILOF (Incremental Local Outlier Factor) method, which uses the LOF metric to determine if a new data point is an
outlier.

item.name: RiLOF
item.description: An outlier detection method that addresses limitations of existing statistical techniques by introducing the MoNNAD metric to label and score query samples.
item.grounding_span:
Degirmenci and Karal [38] introduce RiLOF, which addresses limitations in existing statistical outlier detection
techniques by introducing the MoNNAD (Median of Nearest Neighborhood Absolute Deviation) metric.

item.name: MoNNAD (Median of Nearest Neighborhood Absolute Deviation)
item.description: The median of the absolute variances among the LOF values of the k-nearest neighboring data points and the LOF value of a given sample.
item.grounding_span:
Degirmenci and Karal [38] introduce RiLOF, which addresses limitations in existing statistical outlier detection
techniques by introducing the MoNNAD (Median of Nearest Neighborhood Absolute Deviation) metric.

item.name: GESD (Generalized Extreme Studentized Deviation)
item.description: An outlier detection technique that evaluates the maximum absolute difference between each sample and the dataset mean, normalized by the standard deviation.
item.grounding_span:
The GESD (Generalized Extreme Studentized Deviation) technique, as introduced by Rosner [118], and the MAD
(Median Absolute Deviation) technique, proposed by Leys et al. [82], are both outlier detection methods that share
similarities in their underlying principles.

item.name: MAD (Median Absolute Deviation)
item.description: An outlier detection technique using the median of absolute differences between data records and the dataset median, with a constant assuming normally distributed data.
item.grounding_span:
The GESD (Generalized Extreme Studentized Deviation) technique, as introduced by Rosner [118], and the MAD
(Median Absolute Deviation) technique, proposed by Leys et al. [82], are both outlier detection methods that share
similarities in their underlying principles.

item.name: Z-score method
item.description: Normalizes sample values using the mean and standard deviation, or MAD, to detect outliers.
item.grounding_span:
Additionally, the Z-score
method aligns with this principle by normalizing sample values using the mean and standard deviation or MAD.

item.name: robust Z-score version
item.description: A Z-score variant substituting the median and MAD for the mean and standard deviation to obtain more robust measures.
item.grounding_span:
The
robust Z-score version, introduced by Rousseeuw and Hubert [119], substitutes the median and MAD for more robust
measures, demonstrating the shared concept of using statistical measures to detect outliers in datasets.

Based on the knowledge gathered in this survey, we propose a high level taxonomy of metrics.

We categorize the
AI-ready data assessment metrics into six pillars.

Of these categories of metrics, the first four, i.e., data
quality, understandability and usability, structure and
organization, and data governance, are agnostic to the AI
method.

models is accurate, complete, and consistent.

item.grounding_span:
A diverse
set of stakeholders—representing academia, industry, funding agencies, and scholarly publishers —have
come together to design and jointly endorse a concise and measureable set of principles that we refer
to as the FAIR Data Principles.

Beyond proper collection, annotation, and archival, data

should be discovered and re-used for downstream investigations, either alone, or in combination with
newly generated data.

Supporting discovery through good data management
Good data management is not a goal in itself, but rather is the key conduit leading to knowledge
discovery and innovation, and to subsequent data and knowledge integration and reuse by the
community after the data publication process.

What constitutes ‘good data management ’ is, however, largely
undeﬁned, and is generally left as a decision for the data or repository owner.

These ‘computational stakeholders’ are increasingly relevant, and demand
as much, or more, attention as their importance grows.

Many important datasets emerging from traditional, low-throughput bench science don ’t
ﬁt in the data models of these special-purpose repositories, yet these datasets are no less important
with respect to integrative research, reproducibility, and reuse in general.

repositories accept a wide range of data types in a wide variety of formats, generally do not attempt

descriptors of the data deposition.

item.name: machine actionable
item.description: A continuum of states in which a digital object exposes progressively more information to an autonomous computational consumer.
item.grounding_span:
Throughout this paper, we use the phrase ‘machine actionable ’ to indicate a continuum of possible
states wherein a digital object provides increasingly more detailed information to an autonomously-
acting, computational data explorer.

item.name: digital object
item.description: The unit a computational agent encounters and must type, parse, evaluate for usefulness and usability, and act upon.
item.grounding_span:
For example, a machine may be capable of determining the data-type of a discovered digital object,
but not capable of parsing it due to it being in an unknown format; or it may be capable of processing
the contained data, but not capable of determining the licensing requirements related to the retrieval
and/or use of that data.

item.name: computational data explorer

item.grounding_span:

acting, computational data explorer.

item.name: general-purpose repositories

unpredictable.

item.name: FAIR Principles
item.description: The set of guiding principles rendering data Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable; presented here as complementary to the JDDCP and the Data Seal of Approval, and as focusing primarily on the data itself.
item.grounding_span:

datasealofapproval.org/media/ﬁler_public/2013/09/27/guidelines_2014-2015.pdf) in that they share
the general aim to render data re-usable for users other than those who originally generated them.

is displayed.

responses, rapidly replacing traditional search engines like Google
and Bing.

item.name: AI search
item.description: The emerging answer layer spread across AI assistants and AI-infused engines that resolves search-like queries.
item.grounding_span:
The emerging “AI search” layer is fragmented across assistants
and engines.

item.name: AI chat tools
item.description: Consumer AI chat assistants whose usage the chunk describes as mainstream and broadly adopted.
item.grounding_span:
Usage of AI chat tools is
now mainstream in many markets; AI summaries on Google mea-
surably alter click-through patterns; and a handful of AI products
(notably ChatGPT and Perplexity) already capture a growing share
of “search intent” questions that never reach the traditional SERP
(Search Engine Results Page).

item.name: zero-click
item.description: A search session that ends without any outbound click, characteristic of AI-summary result pages.
item.grounding_span:
In
a Pew field study of real-world searches, AI summaries appeared
on ∼18% of observed queries; link clicks fell to 8% when a summary
was present vs. 15% without; only ∼1% of clicks occurred inside the
AI box; and ∼26% of such searches ended the session without any
click—a classic “zero-click” outcome [4].

item.name: AI Overviews
item.description: Google's AI-generated summaries on the result page, whose visibility and prevalence third-party SEO panels tracked during early rollouts.
item.grounding_span:
Industry telemetry points
in the same direction during early rollouts, with third-party SEO
panels documenting sharp changes in the visibility and prevalence
of AI Overviews [10].

item.name: traditional SEO
item.description: Classic ranking-oriented search engine optimization, contrasted with GEO's target of AI-generated answers.
item.grounding_span:
Unlike traditional SEO,
GEO addresses the nuanced nature of AI-generated answers, which
often synthesize multiple sources into structured, citation-rich re-
sponses.

item.name: visibility
item.description: The degree to which a content creator's source surfaces inside generative engine responses; the quantity GEO seeks to improve.
item.grounding_span:
Aggarwal et al. [1] introduce Generative Engine Optimization
(GEO), a novel framework to help content creators improve their
visibility in generative engine responses.

item.name: strategic text sequence (STS)
item.description: An optimized token sequence inserted into a product page to raise the chance an LLM recommends that product.
item.grounding_span:
They demonstrate that by inserting a carefully optimized
strategic text sequence (STS) into a product’s information page,
vendors can significantly increase the likelihood of their product
being recommended as the top choice by an LLM.

item.grounding_span:

ChatGPT with ∼81% global share in July 2025 (Perplexity ∼8%,
Microsoft Copilot ∼5%, Gemini ∼2%, Claude ∼1%) [7].

symmetric Coverage@k as the fraction of domains common
to both sets (number of overlaps divided by k).

counts vary, we use the Jaccard index: Domain Overlap =
size of the intersection of domains divided by the size of the
union of domains.

queries (e.g., a 10-prompt industry vertical), we compute
the mean overlap across its member queries to obtain the
vertical-level score for that engine and condition.

The goal is to evaluate how
four major AI search engines (Claude, Gemini, GPT, Perplexity)
differ in the breadth and overlap of domains when responding to
queries in three representative sectors: Auto Repair, Dentists, and
Moving Companies.

Objective.While prior experiments (§5.3) examined verticals
such as automotive and consumer electronics, here we extend the
analysis tolocal service categories.

similar but even sharper contrasts.
